name: Oracle Berkeley DB
tagline: The 1990s-era embedded key-value library, now Oracle-owned, AGPL-licensed and rarely updated.
description: Berkeley DB started at UC Berkeley in 1991, was commercialised by Sleepycat Software and bought by Oracle in 2006. It is an embedded C library offering B-tree, hash, queue and record-number access methods with transactions, write-ahead logging, replication and hot backups, and for decades it was the storage under OpenLDAP, Subversion, sendmail and early MySQL. Oracle relicensed the open-source edition to AGPL-3.0 in 2013, which drove many projects to LMDB or SQLite, and the latest release, 18.1.40, dates from 2020. It still works, but treat it as a legacy dependency.
statusNote: No new release since 18.1.40 (May 2020); Oracle still distributes it under AGPL-3.0 or a commercial license. LMDB or SQLite are the usual replacements.

license.name: GNU AGPL v3 or Oracle commercial license

pricing.notes: AGPL edition free; a commercial license is required to embed it in closed-source distributed software.

scale.notes: Single-process library; built-in replication manager supports primary-replica HA groups.

strengths: Decades of production use with full ACID transactions and recovery
Multiple access methods: B-tree, hash, queue and record number
Built-in replication manager for high availability
Small footprint suitable for appliances and embedded devices
weaknesses: AGPL or paid license makes embedding in proprietary products awkward
No new releases since 2020 and little community activity
Page-level locking and an older design limit concurrency
Many distributions and projects have already removed it
useCases: Maintaining legacy software built on BDB
Embedded appliances with existing BDB code
notIdealFor: Proprietary products unwilling to buy a license
